title: Isolation ribbons & probabilistic autoscale PRD (draft)
summary: Draft product spec for a new Dedicated Capacity feature set: 'isolation ribbons' (soft isolation bands to protect SLOs), a probabilistic autoscaler tuned for spiky LLM workloads, and a tokenized burst leasing API. Goal is to improve latency SLO adherence while enabling controlled burst behavior and easier operational recovery.
goals: Keep p95 latency within SLO for high-tier tenants during common microbursts
Allow tenants to purchase or borrow short-term burst capacity without hard preemption
Provide operators and customers clear visibility and controls over isolation boundaries
Limit cross-tenant noisy-neighbor impact with minimal wasted idle capacity
non_goals: Replace all existing reservation/burst semantics in one release (this is a gradual opt-in)
Solve every long-tail traffic pattern—focus is on microburst and hour-scale seasonality
Implement full per-model kernel-level scheduling here (runtime improvements handled separately)
background_and_user_needs: We routinely see tenants with short, sharp demand spikes that cause p95/p99 latency regressions across shared Dedicated pools. Current options are rigid: large reserved capacity (expensive) or brittle soft-throttles. Customers want: (1) predictable latency for critical paths, (2) a cheap way to handle short bursts, (3) explainable fallback when capacity saturates. Operators want tooling to reason about tradeoffs and to heal noisy tenants quickly.
proposed_solution: Introduce three cooperating features: (A) Isolation ribbons: soft isolation bands layered on top of existing pool topology. Each ribbon is an allocation band (e.g., 60%, 85%, 100%) with progressively stronger isolation and fallback rules. Low ribbons are highly permissive; higher ribbons lock down cross-tenant sharing. (B) Probabilistic autoscaler: an autoscaling policy that predicts microburst arrival probability and grows capacity conservatively using short-lived ephemeral nodes, using a Bayesian posterior over traffic deltas. It favors adding short-lived capacity with fast warm-paths for known hot tenants. (C) Tokenized burst leasing API: tenants can buy/borrow burst tokens with TTL; tokens grant temporary placement into higher ribbons or access to ephemeral nodes. Tokens are metered, refund-friendly, and spill-over aware.
requirements: API: /v1/dedicated/bursts - POST to request burst tokens, GET to view token balance
Control-plane: ribbon definitions per pool (percent bands + eviction/fallback policy), editable via Console and CLI
Autoscaler: ingest per-tenant short-window rates (1s/10s/1m) and prior burst history; produce scale actions with ephemeral lifetimes (1m-30m)
Scheduling: ephemeral nodes must be prioritized for tenants with tokens; scheduler should prefer colocating token-backed slots with tenant state when possible
Observability: trace from request -> ribbon -> node; surface token spend, ribbon saturation, add/remove scale events, and latency heatmaps
Ops runbook: automated escalation for ribbon over-saturation, rollback knobs to disable probabilistic add/remove, and a quota drain procedure
Billing: token pricing model, backfill refunds for unused token minutes, and billing events emitted to usage pipeline
success_metrics: Reduce p95 latency violations during microburst windows by 40% for top-100 tenants within 3 months of rollout
Decrease overall reserved-capacity spend among pilot customers by 12% via tokenized bursts
Mean time to containment for noisy neighbor incidents reduced from 28m to under 10m with ribbons + telemetry
Operator-triggered emergency pool evictions reduced by 50%
rollout_plan: Phase 1: internal dogfood on a small dedicated cluster (team-owned tenants) to validate ribbon semantics and autoscaler safe-shutdown. Phase 2: invite pilot customers (3–5) with non-critical workloads, enable token purchase via UI only. Phase 3: expand tokens to self-serve purchase and add API stability guarantees. Each phase includes a one-week canary window and automated rollback conditions (sustained p99 > baseline or token mischarging).
open_questions: Appropriate TTL ranges for ephemeral nodes vs. token lifetime—should tokens map 1:1 to node minutes or to admission credits?
How to price tokens such that heavy burst users are disincentivized from permanent dependency?
Interactions with Dedicated's existing soft-eviction policies—should ribbons override preemptibility?
Edge case: when ephemeral add fails (slow warm), should we auto-fallback tenants to hosted models or degrade fidelity?
implementation_notes: Engineering will coordinate three squads: serving-runtime (fast warm paths + scheduling hints), platform-autoscale (probabilistic model + ephemeral lifecycle), and console/billing (token storefront, UI). Short prototype plan: (1) implement ribbon metadata in control-plane and scheduler hookpoints (2 weeks), (2) add token ledger service (1 week), (3) wire ephemeral node lifecycle and fast-warm mechanism (3–4 weeks), (4) autoscaler model iteration with synthetic spike bench (2 weeks). Expect cross-team integration tests and a chaos scenario runbook.
safety_and_sla_considerations: Ribbons are soft—do not violate hard tenancy or data isolation. Ephemeral nodes must honor tenant data controls and KMS boundaries. Autoscaler conservative defaults: do not remove reserved capacity beneath explicit customer reservations; ephemeral nodes are opportunistic and should have a rapid drain path. Billing must never charge users before successful token allocation; all token operations should be idempotent. Add monitoring alerts for unexpected ribbon thrashing and token double-spend.
notes_to_reviewers: Looking for feedback on ribbon band thresholds and the tradeoff curve between aggressive ephemerals vs. increased cost. Also want opinions on token pricing models (subscription vs. on-demand credits). Please reference linked artifacts for existing autoscale prototypes and the warm-path runtime PR. Tag comments inline in Confluence-5467.
